newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian warns of further delays in space station.
newsitem.headline: Russian warns of further delays in space station.

text.p: A Russian space official said on Wednesday Moscow could be late in releasing funds it has promised for building an international space station, despite a U.S. critic's warnings that more delays could kill the project.

Anatoly Kiselyov, head of Moscow's Khrunichev space centre, expressed his fears after nervously showing U.S. legislator James Sensenbrenner the Alpha space station's unfinished "service module", or living quarters, being built at his centre.

Kiselyov told Sensenbrenner the module would be launched according to a recently revised schedule. But he later expressed fears that the Russian government would not provide funds which it has promised to pay by the end of this month.
"If we don't get at least $10 million by the end of February, I won't be able to keep to schedule," he told reporters after Sensenbrenner had left.
The Alpha space station is intended to replace Russia's ageing Mir station as man's primary long-term home in space.
The United States, the European Space Agency, Canada, Italy and Japan are also involved in the Alpha project, and aim to complete the space station early in the next century.

But a cash shortage has put Russia's participation in doubt and raised questions about the whole project. A Russian space official said last month that about $270 million were needed to complete the module.
"The entire programme has been placed in jeopardy," said Sensenbrenner, chairman of the U.S. House of Representatives' Science Committee and a fierce critic of Russia's contribution.

"The problem is with the service module, which if not finished on time will unravel the whole project...From what I have been able to see, there has not been a lot of progress on the service module in the last year."

Sensenbrenner, a legislator from Wisconsin, said U.S. taxpayers were paying $18 billion for the project and that the countries sponsoring Alpha would have to decide by the end of March whether to exclude Russia from the project.
Kiselyov, clearly agitated, said his centre was not to blame for the delays. "I am only responsible for the work of my company," he said. "I am not the president of Russia."

Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin told U.S. Vice President Al Gore earlier this month that Russia would allocate another $100 million by the end of February and $250 million by the end of this year to complete the service module.

But the Russian government, struggling to lead the country out of economic crisis, owes money to almost all branches of the economy. The Khrunichev centre continues to pay its workers, but has delayed production because of cash shortfalls.
Gore and U.S. NASA space officials want to continue working with Russia, but Sensenbrenner can influence the project through his position in the Republican-controlled U.S. Congress.

Russia has already built one module for Alpha with U.S. funding. That module is undergoing its final tests at Khrunichev and is scheduled to go into orbit on November 22. Other sections of the station sare to be attached in stages by 2003.
The service module was originally scheduled for launching in April 1998, but Kiselyov said it was now slated for a six to eight months delay if it gets government funding soon.
"It's just an empty hunk right now," Yevgeny Orlov, the engineer in charge of testing, said as several workers in white coats inspected bolts on the exterior.
Although the vast hangers of the Khrunichev filled with rockets and capsules are testimony to the impressive Russian past in space exploration, there are also signs of decay.
"Quality is the con ern of all," a slogan near the entrance reads, a letter missing from the word concern.
